title: Father Tiber, receive this soldier
author: Livy
setting: The Sublician bridge, Rome, in the war with Porsenna (traditionally late 6th century BC)

source_text: tum Cocles "Tiberine pater" inquit, "te sancte precor, haec arma et hunc militem propitio flumine accipias." ita sicut erat armatus in Tiberim desiluit multisque superincidentibus telis incolumis ad suos tranavit rem ausus plus famae habituram ad posteros quam fidei.
excerpt_note: The first two sentences of section 2.10.11 (the section ends with the start of the next sentence, grata erga tantam virtutem civitas fuit). In the digital file two words of this section carry OCR corrections, Codes → Cocles and tur → tum; the corrected readings are given. The edition prints erat in italic type, which in this Teubner text marks a word added or changed by the editors rather than found in the manuscripts; the Oxford (Conway–Walters) and Loeb (Foster) texts read ita sic armatus. The Perseus file's own header warns that its OCR correction "appears poor and many misprints remain", so this text was compared word for word with Perseus's digital texts of the Loeb edition (B. O. Foster, 1919/1922; file perseus-lat4) and the Oxford edition (Conway and Walters; file perseus-lat3). Apart from that they agree word for word, and both put a comma after tranavit.

macrons.note: Macrons are editorial: added by Vocābula, not printed in the edition. Vowel quantities follow the app lexicon (Wheelock / DCC spellings) where the word is in it, and standard dictionary quantities otherwise.
uncertain: Cocles: both vowels short (like mīles, mīlitis); not machine-checked.
Tiberīne: long ī, as in Tiberīnus; not machine-checked.
sānctē: long ā, as in the app's sānctus, and long final ē of the adverb; not machine-checked.
trānāvit: long ā in trāns-/trā- and in the perfect ending; not machine-checked.
dēsiluit: long ē in dē-; the i is short; not machine-checked.
fideī: short e in fideī (fidēs, 5th declension, after a consonant); not machine-checked.

translation: Then Cocles said, "Father Tiber, I solemnly pray you: receive these arms and this soldier with a kindly stream." So, armed just as he was, he leapt down into the Tiber and, with many missiles falling on him, swam across unharmed to his own side, having dared a deed that would win more fame than belief among later generations.
translation_note: accipiās depends on precor without ut ("I pray [that] you receive"). multīs ... superincidentibus tēlīs is an ablative absolute. In rem ausus plus fāmae habitūram ad posterōs quam fideī, Livy steps outside the story: habitūram (future participle) agrees with rem, and fāmae and fideī are both partitive genitives with plūs.

essay.t: After the Tarquins were expelled, Livy says, they took refuge with Lars Porsenna, king of Clusium, and urged him to restore them; an Etruscan army then marched on Rome.
When the Janiculum hill fell to a sudden attack, only the Sublician bridge stood between the enemy and the city.

Horatius Cocles, on guard there, told his fleeing comrades to break the bridge down behind him, held its head first with Spurius Larcius and Titus Herminius, then sent them back and faced the Etruscans alone until the bridge crashed down.
Then came the prayer to Father Tiber and the swim to safety; the grateful state set up his statue in the comitium and gave him as much land as he could plough round in a day.
Livy himself warns, in the passage, that the deed would have more fame than belief among later generations.
Polybius, a Greek historian writing in the 2nd century BC and the earliest known teller of the story, gives it a different ending.
In his version Horatius, with no companions mentioned and badly wounded, holds the enemy while the bridge is cut, then plunges into the river in full armour and deliberately gives up his life.
Polybius tells it as one example among many, to show the eager rivalry for noble deeds that Roman customs, such as funeral speeches praising the dead, bred in the young.

Britannica calls Horatius perhaps legendary, says the versions differ on whether he reached safety or drowned, and reports a theory that the story grew up to explain an old statue of a lame, one-eyed man in the nearby Temple of Vulcan, which may have represented Vulcan himself.

Livy's preface (praef. 10) explains what such stories are for: the reader should study examples of every kind, set out as on a conspicuous monument, and take from them what to imitate and what to avoid.
Seen that way, the two endings teach different lessons, survival through divine favour in Livy and self-sacrifice in Polybius; the contrast is my own reading.

questions.q: How does the story end in Polybius?
options: He leaps into the river in armour and gives up his life
He swims back to safety and is rewarded with land
He is captured by Porsenna and sent back to Rome
He is elected consul for holding the bridge alone

questions.q: What does Livy say about the deed's credibility?
options: It would win more fame than belief with later generations
He had seen an inscription recording it himself
Polybius had confirmed every detail of the story
The whole Etruscan army saw it, so it is certain

questions.q: According to Livy, how did the state reward Horatius?
options: A statue and as much land as he could plough round in a day
A triumph and the consulship for the following year
A gold crown and a house of his own on the Palatine
Nothing, since the state was too poor to reward him
